basic_identification.full_title: Recommended Practice for Safeguarding Against Warpage and Distortion of Hot Dip Galvanized Articles
basic_identification.sector_category: Metallurgical Engineering / Corrosion Protection (approved by the Metallurgical Engineering Division Council and finalized by the Hot Dip Sprayed and Diffusion Coatings Sectional Committee of the Bureau of Indian Standards)

sectional_committee.name: Hot Dip Sprayed and Diffusion Coatings Sectional Committee

scope.summary: This standard prescribes recommended design principles, fabrication practices, and process control measures to safeguard fabricated iron and steel assemblies against warpage, twisting, and physical distortion during hot-dip zinc galvanizing. It addresses the release of residual stresses, thermal expansion differentials, and cross-section symmetry.

certification_and_marking.standard_type: Code of Practice / Recommended Guidelines (Metallurgical Engineering / Corrosion Protection)
certification_and_marking.certification_status: Voluntary Engineering Code of Practice. Since IS 11812:1986 is an engineering guideline rather than a direct manufacturing product, it does not carry a separate mandatory BIS license or ISI certification mark. However, its design rules, stress-relief practices, venting details, and dipping protocols are universally mandated inside all national public works (CPWD), power transmission (PGCIL), railways, and industrial structural steel engineering contracts to prevent on-site mechanical twisting and structural damage during the hot-dip galvanizing process.

requirements.detail: All structural members used in an assembly should be pre-formed accurately to avoid SPRINGING ACTION and forced alignment during fit-up, thereby eliminating built-in mechanical tension that could be released in the zinc bath.

Where massive weldments or heavy clamping forces are involved, the fabricated assembly should be stress-relieved by a suitable low-temperature heat treatment prior to galvanizing to prevent thermal distortion.

Symmetrical cross-sections (such as I-beams, tubes, and pipes) are highly recommended because they distribute heating and cooling forces evenly about both axes. Non-symmetrical sections (such as channels, angles, or assemblies with dissimilar thicknesses) are highly prone to warping.
Corners on sheet metal products such as pans, bins, and containers should be fabricated with a generous radius to minimize localized stress concentration.

Tightly contacting or overlapping steel surfaces must be completely sealed by continuous welding. This prevents the entrapment of pickling acids or flux in crevices, which can cause severe interior rust, non-uniform coating, or build up explosive steam pressures at galvanizing temperatures (815–850°F / 435–455°C) that pose serious injury risks to plant personnel.

Riveting of fabricated parts prior to dipping is not recommended if the kettle size allows single-dip total immersion. Crevices at contacting rivet heads entrap pickling acids, leading to localized rusting.

If a sheet metal or fabricated structure is too large for single-dip kettles, the sheets and framing should be galvanized separately and assembled post-galvanizing using galvanized or aluminum alloy rivets.

Each fabricated article must be submerged with complete safety. Closed hollow shapes (including pipes, structural hollow sections, pressure vessels, footing stiffeners, and gussets) must be provided with clipped or drilled vent holes to prevent air pockets, ensure complete zinc coverage, and facilitate rapid zinc drainage.

Articles should be dipped in a manner that ensures uniform heating and cooling across their sections. Vertical dipping of channel profiles and framing is preferred over horizontal or low-angle immersion.

Slag and flux residues left by coated welding electrodes are chemically inert to standard pickling acids. All weld slag must be removed prior to pickling by chipping, wire brushing, or sand/shot blasting to prevent uncoated bare spots.

For pipe railings, handrails, and similar assemblies, joints must feature open-mitre configurations at all times to allow continuous internal venting and zinc flow. Closed or blind sections are strictly prohibited, and floor flanges should be made of cast or wrought steel instead of cast iron.

plain_language_summary.summary: IS 11812 : 1986 (Reaffirmed 2021) is the national Indian Standard recommended practice specifying design and fabrication guidelines to safeguard fabricated iron and steel assemblies against warpage, twisting, and dimensional distortion when subjected to the high temperatures (815–850°F / 435–455°C) of molten zinc during hot-dip galvanizing. It acts as a crucial quality-control guide for engineers, fabricators, and galvanizers. The standard outlines key design parameters—such as avoiding thin steel sheets welded to heavy framing, using symmetrical structural sections, and stress-relieving heavy welds. It enforces strict procedural controls, including continuous seal-welding of overlapping joints to avoid acid entrapment and explosive steam expansion, drilling mandatory air-vent and zinc-drainage holes in hollow sections, and dipping assemblies vertically to ensure uniform thermal expansion and contraction.
